pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5–6: read and write NUMERALS 0–100 — extending secure 0–20 numeral reading/writing across the full two-digit range, leaning on the regular tens-and-ones pattern of the written system.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.1 'count to 120 ... read and write numerals'; the numeral system to 100 is embedded here and in K.CC.3.
• Operational details — once 0–20 numerals and rote counting to 100 are secure, reading/writing to 100 is mostly about the REGULAR two-digit pattern: the left digit says the tens, the right digit the ones, and decade words map to the tens digit. The persistent trouble spots are the teens/twenties boundary and the said-first-heard-first mismatch (writing 'forty-two' as 24). This is procedural fluency, not yet full place-value reasoning (that is the two-digit-composition topic).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): read two-digit numerals up to 100 on sight. Tier B (5–6): write any number 0–100 as a numeral from dictation. Tier C (6): read and write across a decade boundary (e.g. 79–80) and place/find numerals on a 0–100 grid without error.
bestPractices: Lean on the REGULAR pattern of two-digit numerals with a 100-square / Gattegno chart: the tens digit changes down the columns, the ones digit across the rows, making 0–100 a system rather than 100 things to memorise.

Directly rehearse the hear-it/write-it order for two-digit numbers where speech and writing agree in English above twenty (forty-TWO → 4 then 2) but the teens don't (thirteen) — contrast the two explicitly.
Practise decade boundaries (29→30, 79→80) which is where reading/writing and rote counting most often break down.
Keep numerals connected to quantity/position via a bead string or 0–100 number line so a two-digit numeral means 'this far along', not just two digits.
Give balanced read AND write practice (say-it → write it; show it → read it; point on the grid) to avoid one-way fluency.
keyRepresentations: 100-square and Gattegno tens-and-ones chart exposing the regular two-digit pattern.
0–100 bead string / number line linking each numeral to a position/quantity.
Place-value / arrow (Dienes) cards building 42 as 40 and 2 to reinforce which digit is which.
Decade-boundary number tracks (25–35, 75–85) for the tricky crossings.
commonMisconceptions: Transposing spoken two-digit numbers (writing 'forty-two' as 24) — confusing the ones-first teens with the tens-first pattern of the rest.
Decade-boundary errors when counting/writing (after 29 saying/writing 'twenty-ten', or 39→50).
Reading a two-digit numeral as two separate digits ('four, two' for 42) rather than as forty-two.
Miswriting the 'ty' decades (writing 70 as 17, confusing seventy/seventeen).
Omitting or misplacing 0 in decade numbers (writing 40 as 4, or 'forty' as 400).

learn.summary: For children aged 5–6 extending secure 0–20 numeral reading/writing to the full 0–100 range. The goal is procedural fluency in reading and writing two-digit numerals by exploiting the regular pattern (left digit = tens, right digit = ones), targeting the persistent trouble spots: the spoken-order transposition (writing 'forty-two' as 24), decade-boundary crossings (29→30, 79→80), and keeping the 0 in decade numbers. This is numeral fluency, not yet full place-value reasoning.

activities.title: Hear-it, build-it, place-it on a hundred square
feedback: If a learner writes 24 for 'forty-two', place both 24 and 42 on the grid and show how far apart they sit — the transposed numeral is visibly in the wrong region.

If a learner drops the zero when writing a decade number (writing 40 as 4, or 'forty' as 400), point out that the 0 holds the ones place so forty needs both digits and no extra ones; contrast 4 and 40 on the number line to show they are different sizes.
When a number is placed on the grid, an optional response is to light up the cell so a correct answer settles into the right column/row and a wrong one shows the mismatch in position.
For decade-boundary slips (saying 'twenty-ten' after 29, or 39→50), slow down and count along a bead string or number line so 29→30 is felt as one step forward.
Reinforce by linking the numeral to quantity/position on a bead string or number line so the written symbol stays tied to 'how far along'.
activities.rationale: Letting children act on the regular two-digit system — composing from tens and ones, writing from dictation, and seeing position feedback — is intended to build the pattern actively and to target the transposition, zero-omission and decade-boundary errors. Linking numerals to position/quantity keeps the symbol meaningful. Efficacy is proposed, not established.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals.
A 100-square / Gattegno chart exposes the regular tens-and-ones structure of two-digit numerals; decade boundaries and spoken-order transposition are the key difficulties.
learnerActions: Listen to a spoken two-digit number (e.g. 'sixty-eight') and write or point to its numeral.
Place the numeral in its position on a 100-square (state whether it is a 1–100 or a 0–99 layout), then check whether it lands where that number belongs.
Build a number from tens-and-ones cards: compose 42 by taking the '40' card and placing the '2' over its zero, so the tens and ones are explicitly separated.
Work across decade boundaries: continue 28, 29, __ and 78, 79, __ , writing each numeral (30 and 80).
Do both directions: say-it → write it; show it → read it aloud; point-to-it on the grid.
activities.intendedInsight: 0–100 is one regular system, not a hundred separate facts: moving down a column the tens digit goes up while the ones digit stays the same, and moving along a row the ones digit changes. On a 0–99 square each row shares one tens digit. On a 1–100 square the decade number (10, 20, … 100) ends each row, so it is the one cell in its row with a different tens digit. Either way, each numeral means 'this far along', not just two loose digits.

activities.title: Minimal-pair contrast: -teen versus -ty
feedback: If a learner writes 14 for 'forty', swaps 13/30, or confuses seventeen/seventy (writing 70 as 17), slow the word ending and contrast the pair with base-ten sticks (4 tens versus one ten and 4); firm the decade sequence by rote count.

If dictated teens come out reversed (41 for 'fourteen') while other numbers are fine, treat it as a normal transcription stage: keep modelling teens with a tens/ones frame and let exposure resolve it, rather than marking it wrong repeatedly.
activities.rationale: Minimal pairs isolate the genuine error types — auditory -teen/-ty confusion and teen transposition — so practice targets where fluency breaks rather than re-drilling secure numbers.
sourceClaims: A 100-square / Gattegno chart exposes the regular tens-and-ones structure of two-digit numerals; decade boundaries and spoken-order transposition are the key difficulties.
learnerActions: Read aloud the auditory -teen/-ty pairs: 13 and 30, 14 and 40, 17 and 70 (seventeen/seventy); then the separate reading-order/transposition pair 17 and 71 (seventeen/seventy-one).
Take dictation of 'forty' then 'fourteen'; write each and compare.
Explain or show how 40 and 14 differ, e.g. with base-ten sticks: forty is 4 tens; fourteen is one ten and 4.
Say the endings clearly: contrast the spoken ones-first teens (thir-TEEN) with the spoken tens-first rest (FORTY-two), while noting both are written tens-first (13 and 42).
activities.intendedInsight: The teens 13–19 are SAID with the ones idea first (a special '-teen' word), and eleven and twelve are irregular words. All of them, like every two-digit number, are WRITTEN tens-first (11, 12, 13, 14). Numbers from 20 up are both said and written tens-first. Seeing that teens are spoken in a different order from how they are written helps keep the two patterns apart and supports moving past writing 41 for fourteen as place value develops.

activities.title: Fluency check: read, write, place, order
feedback: A correct answer confirms fluency; a wrong one points back to the build/contrast activities — e.g. a transposition sends the learner to the tens-and-ones card build, a -teen/-ty slip to the minimal-pair contrast, a dropped zero back to placing 4 versus 40.
When a dictated 'forty-two' is written as 24, show the gap between 24 and 42 on the line rather than just marking it wrong.
activities.rationale: Two-digit numeral reading/writing is highly checkable in multiple formats; a check can consolidate and surface which specific trouble spot remains. It tests fluency rather than building the pattern insight, so it follows the active work; it does not by itself teach the pattern.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals.
learnerActions: Write the numeral for a spoken number (e.g. 'forty-two' → 42).
Read a shown numeral aloud (e.g. 68 as 'sixty-eight', not 'six, eight').
Place a numeral on a 0–100 line (e.g. position 68).
Order a short sequence across a decade boundary, e.g. fill the gaps around 29→30.
Write the number that is one more than 19 (20); write 'sixty-two' then 'twenty-six' and check they differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading and writing to 100 should be reliable in both directions and across decade crossings, with minimal pairs kept distinct and the zero kept in decade numbers.

constraints: Secure 0–20 numeral reading/writing and rote counting to 100 are prerequisites before extending to 100.

This is procedural numeral fluency, not full place-value reasoning (two-digit composition/decomposition is a separate topic); keep representations tied to quantity/position but do not assume full place-value understanding.
Writing teen numbers in spoken order (41 for 'fourteen') is a normal developmental transcription stage that matures with place value; do not drill it as a careless error or mark it wrong repeatedly.

A static tappable 100-square is a useful reference and can present a numeral and its word, but it cannot by itself rehearse the productive skills of writing from dictation or free reading; use it as a scaffold alongside writing/speaking practice.
Recognition-only (multiple-choice) responses confirm reading but do not elicit independent numeral writing; include actual writing-from-dictation for the production half of the skill.
Decade numbers keep the 0 as a ones-place holder (40, not 4 or 400); treat zero omission/misplacement as its own error alongside transposition and -teen/-ty confusion.

Teens are written tens-first (13, 14) just like all two-digit numerals; only the SPOKEN order of teens differs, so teach the spoken/written order distinction rather than implying teens are written ones-first.

Position-lighting, grid cells, card-dragging and spoken prompts are optional ways to make feedback concrete, not required mechanisms; the same work can be done on paper, with a bead string, or with spoken dictation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three sources (CCSS-M 1.NBT.1 and the NCETM 100-square guidance) are marked verified:false in the source row; the claims that the 100-square exposes the regular structure and that transposition/decade boundaries are the key difficulties are cited but not independently verified here.

Corrected a factual error in the -teen/-ty activity's intended insight: the candidate stated teens are 'said and written with the ones idea first'. Teens are only SPOKEN ones-first; they are written tens-first (13, 14) like every other two-digit numeral, which is precisely why writing 41 for fourteen is a mismatch error.

The legacy entries asserted 'a static picture cannot rehearse' the skill and '3D adds nothing' for flat symbols; these have been softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal claims, and the 3D dismissal was dropped as unsupported boilerplate.
The original commonMisconception on omitting/misplacing the 0 in decade numbers (40 as 4, 'forty' as 400) is reinstated in activity feedback and constraints.

The source's diagnostic prompt says to watch rather than question the child; this observation framing is retained descriptively, but comparative-efficacy claims about watching versus questioning are not asserted as established.

probeDeeper: Write the number that is one more than 19.
Read this: 40. Now this: 14. Say how you can tell them apart.
assess.correctAnswer: Reads all four correctly and writes 40, 14, 62, 26 — distinguishing 13 from 30 and not transposing 62/26.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the -teen and -ty sounds: writes 14 for 'forty' or reads 30 as 'thirteen'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Slow the ending, contrast the pair with base-ten sticks (forty = 4 tens; fourteen = ten and 4). Firm the decade sequence in rote count.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dictation of 'forty' yields 14, or reading 13/30 aloud swaps them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes teen numbers in spoken order: 41 for 'fourteen' (hears 'four' first)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill it as a careless error or mark it wrong repeatedly — it is a normal transcription stage that resolves as place value matures. Keep modelling teens with a tens/ones frame and let exposure do the work.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dictated teens come out reversed (41, 61) while decades and other two-digit numbers are fine.

responseLevels.gap: Confuses teen/decade pairs or cannot write two-digit numerals from dictation.
responseLevels.full: Reads and writes all numerals 0–100 accurately from dictation and by sight, reliably distinguishing minimal pairs.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes most numerals 0–100 but slips on -teen/-ty minimal pairs or occasionally transposes teens.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch the child read and write. First: 'Read these aloud: 13, 30, 17, 71.' Then dictate for them to write: 'forty … fourteen … sixty-two … twenty-six.' Watch the minimal pairs (13/30, 14/40, 62/26) rather than asking them about the numbers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The contrasting minimal pairs isolate the two real errors: -teen/-ty auditory confusion (40 vs 14) and teen transposition (writing 41 for fourteen). A child who has the numeral system handles both directions; watching, not questioning, catches the slip in the act.
